prologue.speaker: narrator
prologue.text: The Alchemist's Tower once trained the best chemists in the land. Every floor had a teacher, and every teacher asked one question above all others: WHY?

prologue.speaker: narrator
prologue.text: Then its greatest teacher, Magister Mordant, decided 'why' was a waste of time. He had his students memorize answers instead. Faster, he said.

prologue.speaker: narrator
prologue.text: His shortcut students mixed reagents they didn't understand. The explosion blew the top clean off the tower. Mordant was never seen again... at least, not alive.

prologue.speaker: narrator
prologue.text: Now his ghost haunts every floor, twisting the lessons into flashcards. Climb the tower, learn the WHY, and set things right.

c2h7-h2bonds.desc: Claim: hydrogen forms two covalent bonds.

ions.name: Ions

diff-elements.name: Different Elements

rule-aufbau.name: Aufbau Principle
rule-aufbau.desc: The lowest-energy orbitals fill up first: 1s, 2s, 2p, 3s, 3p, 4s, 3d...

rule-pauli.name: Pauli Exclusion
rule-pauli.desc: Only two electrons can share an orbital, and they must have opposite spins.

rule-hund.name: Hund's Rule
rule-hund.desc: When orbitals have equal energy, electrons go one per orbital with parallel spins before any pair up.

rule-octet.name: Octet Rule
rule-octet.desc: Main-group atoms are especially stable with 8 valence electrons (an octet).

shell-8.name: 8 Electrons
shell-8.desc: 8 electrons: enough to fill four orbitals.

shell-2.name: 2 Electrons
shell-2.desc: 2 electrons: enough to fill one orbital.

shell-18.name: 18 Electrons
shell-18.desc: 18 electrons: enough to fill nine orbitals.

shell-6.name: 6 Electrons
shell-6.desc: 6 electrons: enough to fill three orbitals.

shape-p.name: Dumbbell
shape-p.desc: A dumbbell: two lobes on opposite sides of the nucleus.

shape-s.name: Sphere
shape-s.desc: A sphere centered on the nucleus.

shape-hybrid.name: Lopsided Lobes
shape-hybrid.desc: Two unequal lobes: one big, one small.

bond-sigma.name: σ (Sigma) Bond
bond-sigma.desc: A bond from head-on overlap along the line between nuclei. It's cylindrically symmetric. Every single bond is σ.

bond-pi.name: π (Pi) Bond
bond-pi.desc: A bond from sideways overlap of p orbitals. Its electron density sits above and below the bond axis.

bond-ionic.name: Ionic Bond
bond-ionic.desc: Electrical attraction between oppositely charged ions, like Na⁺ Cl⁻. No electrons are shared.

mo-bonding.name: Bonding MO
mo-bonding.desc: Molecular orbital from the additive combination of atomic orbitals. Lower in energy; electrons here hold the nuclei together.

mo-anti.name: Antibonding MO
mo-anti.desc: Molecular orbital from the subtractive combination. Higher in energy, with a node between the nuclei.

h2-1s-headon.name: 1s + 1s Head-On
h2-1s-headon.desc: Two singly occupied 1s orbitals overlap head-on, pairing their electrons in a σ bond.

h2-p-side.name: p + p Sideways
h2-p-side.desc: Sideways overlap of two p orbitals makes a π bond.

h2-transfer.name: Electron Transfer
h2-transfer.desc: One atom gives an electron to the other, making ions. That's ionic bonding.

mo-both-bonding.name: Both in Bonding MO
mo-both-bonding.desc: Both electrons go into the bonding MO.

mo-split.name: One in Each MO
mo-split.desc: One electron goes into the bonding MO, one into the antibonding MO.

mo-both-anti.name: Both in Antibonding
mo-both-anti.desc: Both electrons go into the antibonding MO.

mo-atomic.name: Stay on Their Atoms
mo-atomic.desc: Each electron stays in its own atom's 1s orbital.

node-zero.name: Zero Electron Density
node-zero.desc: A node: a region where the electron density is zero, like the plane between the two lobes of a p orbital.

node-nucleus.name: The Nucleus
node-nucleus.desc: The dense, positively charged center of an atom.

node-max.name: Max Electron Density
node-max.desc: A region of maximum electron density.

node-overlap.name: Orbital Overlap Zone
node-overlap.desc: The region where two orbitals overlap.

hyb-sp3.name: sp³
hyb-sp3.desc: One s + three p orbitals make four sp³ hybrids pointing to the corners of a tetrahedron, 109.5° apart. Four σ bonds/lone pairs.

hyb-sp2.name: sp²
hyb-sp2.desc: One s + two p orbitals make three sp² hybrids in a flat plane, 120° apart. One p orbital is left over for a π bond.

hyb-sp.name: sp
hyb-sp.desc: One s + one p orbital make two sp hybrids 180° apart (linear). Two p orbitals are left over for two π bonds.

hyb-p.name: Plain p (No Hybrid)
hyb-p.desc: Plain, unmixed p orbitals, which sit 90° apart.

ang-180.desc: A straight line: the linear angle.

geo-planar120.name: Flat, 120°
geo-planar120.desc: Trigonal planar: all atoms in one plane, bonds 120° apart. Typical of sp² atoms.

geo-tetra.name: Tetrahedral, 109.5°
geo-tetra.desc: Four groups pointing to the corners of a tetrahedron. Typical of sp³ atoms.

geo-linear.name: Linear, 180°
geo-linear.desc: Atoms in a straight line. Typical of sp atoms.

bl-triple.name: C≡C (Acetylene)
bl-triple.desc: A carbon–carbon triple bond, as in acetylene.

bl-double.name: C=C (Ethylene)
bl-double.desc: A carbon–carbon double bond, as in ethylene.

bl-single.name: C–C (Ethane)
bl-single.desc: A carbon–carbon single bond, as in ethane.

tb-1s2p.name: 1 σ + 2 π
tb-1s2p.desc: One σ bond plus two π bonds.

tb-2s1p.name: 2 σ + 1 π
tb-2s1p.desc: Two σ bonds plus one π bond.

db-pi-weaker.name: π Overlap Is Weaker
db-pi-weaker.desc: Claim: the π part of a double bond, made by sideways overlap, is weaker than the σ part.

db-longer.name: Double Bonds Are Longer
db-longer.desc: Claim: double bonds are longer than single bonds.

db-two-sigma.name: Two Crowded σ Bonds
db-two-sigma.desc: Claim: a double bond is two σ bonds crowding each other.

db-sigma-weak.name: Its σ Bond Is Weak
db-sigma-weak.desc: Claim: the σ part of a double bond is unusually weak.

sp3-3e.name: 3 Electrons per Hybrid
sp3-3e.desc: Reading: each hybrid orbital holds 3 electrons.

sp3-shell3.name: Third Shell
sp3-shell3.desc: Reading: the orbitals come from the third shell.

lp-sp3-2.name: sp³, 2 Lone Pairs
lp-sp3-2.desc: sp³ hybridized, with two lone pairs.

lp-sp3-1.name: sp³, 1 Lone Pair
lp-sp3-1.desc: sp³ hybridized, with one lone pair.

lp-sp2-2.name: sp², 2 Lone Pairs
lp-sp2-2.desc: sp² hybridized, with two lone pairs.

lp-sp-2.name: sp, 2 Lone Pairs
lp-sp-2.desc: sp hybridized, with two lone pairs.

hyb-none.name: Can't Hybridize
hyb-none.desc: Claim: this atom doesn't use hybrid orbitals.

geo-bent.name: Bent, Near 109°
geo-bent.desc: Bent: two bonds meeting at an angle near 109°.

benz-planar-sp2.name: Flat Ring, All sp²
benz-planar-sp2.desc: A flat ring of sp² carbons.

benz-pucker-sp3.name: Puckered Ring, All sp³
benz-pucker-sp3.desc: A puckered ring of sp³ carbons.

benz-planar-sp.name: Flat Ring, All sp
benz-planar-sp.desc: A flat ring of sp carbons.

benz-alt.name: Alternating sp³/sp²
benz-alt.desc: A ring alternating sp³ and sp² carbons.

skel-ends.name: Every End & Corner
skel-ends.desc: Claim: a carbon sits at every line end and every place lines meet.

skel-written.name: Only Where Written
skel-written.desc: Claim: carbons are only where a "C" is written.

skel-endsonly.name: Only at Line Ends
skel-endsonly.desc: Claim: carbons are only at the ends of lines.

skel-cornersonly.name: Only at Corners
skel-cornersonly.desc: Claim: carbons are only where lines meet.

hc-ch3.desc: A carbon carrying 3 hydrogens (a methyl group).

skel-hetero.name: Non-C Atoms + Their H's
skel-hetero.desc: Claim: everything except carbons and the H's on carbons is written out.

skel-onlyc.name: Only Carbons
skel-onlyc.desc: Claim: only the carbons are written out.

skel-every.name: Every Atom
skel-every.desc: Claim: every atom, H's included, is written out.

skel-charged.name: Only Charged Atoms
skel-charged.desc: Claim: only atoms with a charge are written out.

s-butane.name: Butane
s-butane.desc: CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₃, C₄H₁₀. A straight chain of four carbons.

s-isobutane.name: Isobutane
s-isobutane.desc: (CH₃)₃CH, also C₄H₁₀. Same formula as butane, but branched: a different compound.

s-pentane.name: Pentane
s-pentane.desc: CH₃(CH₂)₃CH₃, C₅H₁₂. Five carbons in a row.

s-1butene.name: 1-Butene
s-1butene.desc: CH₂=CHCH₂CH₃, C₄H₈. Four carbons with a double bond.

s-dme.name: Dimethyl Ether

s-ethanol.name: Ethanol

s-acetaldehyde.name: Acetaldehyde

s-propene.name: Propene

s-cyclopropane.name: Cyclopropane
s-cyclopropane.desc: C₃H₆. Three carbons in a ring, all single bonds.

s-propyne.name: Propyne
s-propyne.desc: HC≡CCH₃, C₃H₄. Three carbons with a triple bond.

s-methylamine.name: Methylamine
s-methylamine.desc: CH₃NH₂, CH₅N. Smells like rotting fish!

s-methanimine.name: Methanimine
s-methanimine.desc: CH₂=NH, CH₃N. Has a C=N double bond.

s-2mebutane.name: 2-Methylbutane
s-2mebutane.desc: (CH₃)₂CHCH₂CH₃, C₅H₁₂. A four-carbon chain with a methyl branch on carbon 2.

s-neopentane.name: 2,2-Dimethylpropane
s-neopentane.desc: C(CH₃)₄, C₅H₁₂. One central carbon bonded to four CH₃ groups.

s-vinylcl.name: Vinyl Chloride
s-vinylcl.desc: CH₂=CHCl, C₂H₃Cl. Starting material for PVC plastic.

s-chloroacetylene.name: Chloroacetylene
s-chloroacetylene.desc: HC≡CCl, C₂HCl. Has a triple bond.

ch5-5bonds.name: C Would Need 5 Bonds
ch5-5bonds.desc: Claim: the carbon would need five bonds.

ch5-toolight.name: Too Few Atoms
ch5-toolight.desc: Claim: the molecule has too few atoms to be stable.

ch5-noh.name: C–H Bonds Too Weak
ch5-noh.desc: Claim: C–H bonds are too weak to hold five H's.

lesson.text: Ah, a new student! Come in, come in. Mind the dots on the floor. I'm Professor Lewis Dott, and I draw dots on EVERYTHING. Each dot is an electron, you see.

First, how this tower works. Each problem deals you a hand of cards. Grab a card, drag it, and drop it on a glowing slot. Hover over a card to read its description. Those descriptions are study notes, so read them!
Pick wrong and you lose a heart ♥, but the card flips over and tells you WHY it was wrong. Lose all your hearts and you restart the level. Don't worry, every mistake teaches you something.

You'll also collect POWER cards: Hint calls me back for a nudge, Eliminate throws out a wrong card and explains it, Heal restores a heart, and Shield blocks your next mistake. Use them from the bar at the bottom.
Right answers earn coins, and streaks earn bonus coins. Spend them in the shop between levels. Finish with no mistakes, no hints, and good speed for 3 stars. There's no timer, so take your time.

Now, chemistry! Organic chemistry is the study of carbon compounds. Why carbon? Carbon is in group 4A: it has 4 valence electrons and needs 4 more to fill its octet. So carbon forms 4 bonds. We call that 'tetravalent'.

Here's the trick for counting bonds: count how many electrons an atom is SHORT of an octet. H has 1 and needs 1 → 1 bond. C needs 4 → 4 bonds. N has 5, needs 3 → 3 bonds. O has 6, needs 2 → 2 bonds. Halogens have 7, need 1 → 1 bond.

Worked example from the book: how many H's does phosphorus bond to in phosphine? Phosphorus is in group 5A, like nitrogen. 5 valence electrons, needs 3 more... so PH₃! Leftover valence electrons sit as lone pairs, like the one pair on N in NH₃.

problems.prompt: How many covalent bonds does carbon usually form?
problems.hint: Count how many electrons carbon is short of an octet.

explain.n-bonds-4: Right! Carbon has 4 valence electrons (2s² 2p²) and needs 4 more to reach neon's octet, so it shares 4 pairs: 4 bonds.
explain.n-bonds-2: Tempting, since ground-state carbon has only 2 unpaired electrons (2p²). But carbon actually forms 4 bonds. It needs 4 more electrons to complete its octet. (Hybridization in 1.6 explains how.)
explain.n-bonds-3: Three bonds is nitrogen's pattern (5 valence electrons, needs 3). Carbon has 4 valence electrons and needs 4 more: 4 bonds.
explain.n-bonds-8: 8 is the number of electrons in an octet, not the number of bonds. Each bond holds 2 shared electrons, so carbon's 4 bonds give it 8 electrons.

problems.prompt: How many hydrogens does phosphorus bond to in phosphine, the simple phosphorus hydride?
problems.hint: Phosphorus is in the same group as nitrogen.

explain.f-ph3: Right! Phosphorus is in group 5A with 5 valence electrons. It needs 3 more for an octet, so it bonds to 3 H's: PH₃. The leftover 2 electrons are a lone pair.
explain.f-ph5: Good thinking that phosphorus CAN expand its octet. It often forms 5 bonds in compounds like phosphates (1.10). But the simple hydride follows the octet rule: 5 valence electrons, needs 3 → PH₃.
explain.f-ph2: With only 2 H's, phosphorus would have 7 valence electrons, one short of an octet. It needs 3 bonds: PH₃.
explain.f-ph4: Neutral PH₄ would give phosphorus 9 valence electrons. (The PH₄⁺ ion exists, but that has a charge.) Group 5A → 3 bonds → PH₃.

problems.prompt: Give the likely formula for each pair of elements. (Based on Problem 1-5.)
problems.hint: Aluminum is in group 3A. How many electrons does it have to share?

explain.f-ccl4: Carbon makes 4 bonds and each chlorine (7 valence electrons) makes 1. So it's CCl₄.
explain.f-alh3: Aluminum is in group 3A with 3 valence electrons, so it forms 3 bonds: AlH₃. (Al ends up with only 6 electrons, which is why AlH₃ and AlCl₃ love grabbing electron pairs.)
explain.f-sif4: Silicon is right below carbon in group 4A, so it bonds like carbon: 4 bonds. SiF₄.
explain.f-alh5: Classic trap: '8 minus 3 = 5'. That trick works for atoms on the RIGHT side (N, O, halogens) that have lots of electrons. Aluminum only has 3 electrons to share, so it forms 3 bonds: AlH₃.
explain.f-ccl2: Carbon with 2 bonds would have only 6 electrons around it. Carbon is tetravalent: 4 bonds, so CCl₄.
explain.f-sif2: Silicon is in carbon's group (4A) and forms 4 bonds, so it's SiF₄, not SiF₂.

problems.prompt: Why can't an organic molecule have the formula C₂H₇? (Problem 1-7)
problems.hint: Count the open bonding spots on two bonded carbons.

explain.c2h7-toomanyh: Right! Two carbons bonded together each have 3 bonds left, which is 6 spots for H. C₂H₆ (ethane) is the max. A 7th H would need a carbon with 5 bonds.
explain.c2h7-h2bonds: Hydrogen has 1 electron and needs just 1 more to match helium, so it always forms exactly 1 bond. The real problem is that two carbons only have room for 6 H's.
explain.c2h7-nocc: Carbon bonding to carbon is totally fine. That's how chains and rings form (Kekulé's big idea). The problem is the hydrogen count: max 6 for two carbons.
explain.c2h7-odd: Odd numbers of atoms are fine (CH₃Cl has 5). The problem is that two carbons can only hold 6 H's.

problems.prompt: How many lone pairs does the nitrogen in ammonia, NH₃, have?
problems.hint: N has 5 valence electrons. How many go into the 3 N–H bonds?

explain.lp-1: Right! N has 5 valence electrons. 3 of them pair up in the three N–H bonds, and the remaining 2 form one lone pair.
explain.lp-0: Nitrogen has 5 valence electrons but uses only 3 in bonds to H. The 2 left over form a lone pair, so there's 1.
explain.lp-2: Two lone pairs is oxygen's pattern (as in water). Nitrogen has 5 valence electrons: 3 for bonds, 2 left = 1 lone pair.
explain.lp-3: Three lone pairs is a halogen's pattern. Nitrogen has 5 valence electrons: 3 in bonds and 2 left over, which is 1 lone pair.

problems.prompt: Which of these atoms normally forms exactly TWO covalent bonds?
problems.hint: Which one is 2 electrons short of an octet?

explain.el-o: Right! Oxygen has 6 valence electrons (2s² 2p⁴) and needs 2 more, so it forms 2 bonds, as in H₂O.
explain.el-n: Nitrogen has 5 valence electrons and needs 3 more, so it forms 3 bonds (NH₃).
explain.el-c: Carbon has 4 valence electrons and needs 4 more, so it forms 4 bonds (CH₄).
explain.el-cl: Chlorine has 7 valence electrons and needs only 1 more, so it forms 1 bond.
explain.el-h: Hydrogen has 1 electron and needs 1 more to match helium, so it forms 1 bond.

lesson.text: Path of Atoms! Let's start small. An atom has a tiny, dense nucleus of protons (+) and neutrons (neutral), surrounded by electrons (−). The atomic number Z counts protons. The mass number A counts protons + neutrons.
Same element, different number of neutrons? Those are ISOTOPES. Carbon-12 and carbon-13 both have 6 protons. Carbon-13 just has one more neutron.

Electrons live in ORBITALS: regions where an electron spends 90–95% of its time. s orbitals are spheres. p orbitals are dumbbells with two lobes and a NODE between them, a spot with zero electron density.
Orbitals come in shells. Shell 1: one 1s orbital (2 electrons). Shell 2: one 2s + three 2p (8 electrons). Shell 3: 3s + three 3p + five 3d (18 electrons). Each orbital holds 2 electrons, max.

Three rules fill them. AUFBAU: lowest energy first (1s, 2s, 2p, 3s, 3p, 4s, 3d). PAULI: max two electrons per orbital, opposite spins. HUND: equal-energy orbitals get one electron each, spins parallel, before any pair up.

Worked example: carbon has 6 electrons. 1s gets 2, 2s gets 2, and the last 2 go into the 2p orbitals one at a time (Hund!). That's 1s² 2s² 2p². The superscripts are electron counts, so they always add up to Z.

problems.prompt: Carbon-12 and carbon-13 have the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons. They are...
problems.hint: Same atomic number, different mass number.

explain.isotopes: Right! Isotopes have the same atomic number (6 protons for carbon) but different mass numbers because their neutron counts differ.
explain.ions: Ions differ in ELECTRONS, which gives them a charge. Carbon-12 and carbon-13 differ in neutrons, so they're isotopes.
explain.isomers: Isomers are different COMPOUNDS with the same formula, which is a molecule-level idea. Atoms that differ only in neutrons are isotopes.
explain.diff-elements: Same number of protons means same element: both are carbon. Different neutrons makes them isotopes.

problems.prompt: What is the ground-state electron configuration of oxygen (Z = 8)? (Problem 1-1a)
problems.hint: The superscripts must add up to 8.

explain.cfg-ne: That adds up to 10 electrons, which is neon (or the O²⁻ ion). Neutral oxygen has 8: 1s² 2s² 2p⁴.
explain.cfg-skip2s: This skips 2s. By the Aufbau principle, 2s is lower in energy than 2p and fills first. Oxygen is 1s² 2s² 2p⁴.
explain.cfg-c: That's only 6 electrons, which is carbon. Oxygen has 8: 1s² 2s² 2p⁴.

problems.prompt: What is the ground-state electron configuration of nitrogen (Z = 7)? (Problem 1-1b)
problems.hint: Total of 7 electrons, and no orbital holds more than 2.

explain.cfg-n: Right! 2 + 2 + 3 = 7. By Hund's rule, the three 2p electrons spread out, one in each p orbital, spins parallel.
explain.cfg-2s3: An s subshell is ONE orbital, and by the Pauli exclusion principle one orbital holds at most 2 electrons. 2s³ is impossible.
explain.cfg-o: That's 8 electrons, which is oxygen. Nitrogen has 7: 1s² 2s² 2p³.
explain.cfg-f: That's 9 electrons, which is fluorine. Nitrogen has 7: 1s² 2s² 2p³.

problems.prompt: What is the ground-state electron configuration of sulfur (Z = 16)? (Problem 1-1c)
problems.hint: After 3s comes 3p, and the total must be 16.

explain.cfg-s: Right! 2 + 2 + 6 + 2 + 4 = 16. Notice the outer shell, 3s² 3p⁴, looks just like oxygen's 2s² 2p⁴. Same group, same pattern.
explain.cfg-ar: That's 18 electrons, which is argon. Sulfur has 16, so 3p only gets 4: 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁴.
explain.cfg-s3d: This jumps to 3d before filling 3p. 3p is lower in energy, so it fills first (Aufbau). Sulfur is 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁴.
explain.cfg-o: That's oxygen, with 8 electrons. Sulfur is in the same group but one row down, with 16 electrons.

problems.prompt: Match each electron-filling rule to its name.

slots.label: Max 2 electrons per orbital, opposite spins
Equal-energy orbitals: one electron each before pairing

problems.hint: 'Aufbau' is German for 'building up'.

explain.rule-aufbau: The Aufbau ('building up') principle: fill orbitals from lowest energy up. It goes on the 'lowest-energy first' slot.
explain.rule-pauli: The Pauli exclusion principle: only two electrons per orbital, with opposite spins (↑↓). It goes on the 'max 2 electrons' slot.
explain.rule-hund: Hund's rule: in equal-energy orbitals (like the three 2p's), electrons spread out one per orbital with parallel spins before pairing. It goes on the 'one each before pairing' slot.
explain.rule-octet: The octet rule is about why atoms BOND (to reach 8 valence electrons), not about the order orbitals fill in. It doesn't match any of these.

problems.prompt: How many electrons can the second shell hold?
problems.hint: Shell 2 has one s orbital and three p orbitals.

explain.shell-8: Right! One 2s orbital + three 2p orbitals = 4 orbitals × 2 electrons = 8. That's where the octet comes from!
explain.shell-2: That's the FIRST shell, which has only a 1s orbital. Shell 2 has 2s + three 2p = 8 electrons.
explain.shell-18: That's the THIRD shell (3s + three 3p + five 3d). Shell 2 has no d orbitals: 8 electrons.
explain.shell-6: That's just the three 2p orbitals. Don't forget the 2s orbital: 2 + 6 = 8.

problems.prompt: What shape is a p orbital?
problems.hint: Think of two lobes with a node in between.

explain.shape-p: Right! A p orbital is dumbbell-shaped: two lobes with opposite algebraic signs, separated by a node at the nucleus.
explain.shape-s: Spherical is the s orbital. A p orbital is a dumbbell with two lobes.
explain.shape-d: Cloverleaf is the shape of four of the five d orbitals. A p orbital has just two lobes.
explain.shape-hybrid: One big lobe and one small lobe is a HYBRID orbital like sp³ (1.6). A plain p orbital has two equal-sized lobes.

lesson.text: How do orbitals make bonds? Valence bond theory says a covalent bond forms when a half-filled orbital on one atom overlaps a half-filled orbital on another. The two electrons pair up between the nuclei.
In H₂, two 1s orbitals overlap HEAD-ON. Bonds from head-on overlap are called SIGMA (σ) bonds. Slice one across the middle and you get a circle: they're cylindrically symmetric.

Forming the H–H bond RELEASES 436 kJ/mol. Breaking it ABSORBS 436 kJ/mol. Making bonds always gives off energy, and breaking them always costs energy. The best distance between the nuclei, 74 pm in H₂, is the bond length.

Molecular orbital theory tells it differently. Atomic orbitals combine into MOs that belong to the whole molecule. Adding them gives a lower-energy BONDING MO. Subtracting them gives a higher-energy ANTIBONDING MO with a node between the nuclei.
Sideways overlap of two p orbitals gives a PI (π) bond, with electron density above and below the bond axis. In ethylene's MO picture, the π bonding MO is filled and the π antibonding MO is empty.
Last tip: valence electrons are the ones in the OUTERMOST shell. For selenium, that's 4s² 4p⁴, so 6. The 3d electrons sit in an inner shell, so they don't count as outer-shell electrons.

problems.prompt: How does the H–H bond in H₂ form, according to valence bond theory?
problems.hint: What orbital does a hydrogen atom have its electron in?

explain.h2-1s-headon: Right! Each H has one electron in a 1s orbital. The two 1s orbitals overlap head-on, the electrons pair up, and you get a σ bond.
explain.h2-p-side: Hydrogen has no p electrons. Its only electron is in 1s. Sideways p overlap makes π bonds, which H₂ doesn't have.
explain.h2-transfer: Transferring an electron makes ions (ionic bonding, like Na⁺Cl⁻). In H₂, the two H atoms SHARE electrons in a covalent bond.
explain.h2-2p: Hydrogen's electron is in 1s, not 2p. The H–H bond is 1s–1s head-on overlap.

problems.prompt: When two H atoms form an H₂ molecule, what happens to the energy?
problems.hint: Is H₂ more or less stable than two separate H atoms?

explain.e-release436: Right! H₂ is 436 kJ/mol lower in energy than two separate H atoms, so 436 kJ/mol is released when the bond forms. That's the H–H bond strength.
explain.e-absorb436: 436 kJ/mol is ABSORBED when you BREAK the bond. Forming it does the opposite and releases 436 kJ/mol.
explain.e-release74: 74 is the H–H bond LENGTH (74 pm), not its energy. Forming the bond releases 436 kJ/mol.
explain.e-none: Atoms bond because the result is more stable. Making a bond always releases energy, 436 kJ/mol for H–H.

problems.prompt: Match each description to the bond or orbital it describes.

slots.label: Sideways p overlap; density above & below the axis

problems.hint: The 'anti' MO is the one with a node between the nuclei.

explain.bond-sigma: σ bonds come from head-on overlap along the line between nuclei, so they're cylindrically symmetric (1.5).
explain.bond-pi: π bonds come from sideways overlap of p orbitals. Their electron density sits above and below the internuclear axis (1.8).
explain.mo-bonding: The bonding MO comes from ADDING orbital wave functions. It's lower in energy, and its electrons spend time between the nuclei.
explain.mo-anti: The antibonding MO comes from SUBTRACTING wave functions. It's higher in energy and has a node between the nuclei.
explain.bond-ionic: Ionic bonds are attractions between charged ions. No orbital overlap is involved, so it doesn't match any of these descriptions.

problems.prompt: In the molecular orbital picture of H₂, where do the two electrons go?
problems.hint: Electrons fill the lowest-energy orbital first, two per orbital.

explain.mo-both-bonding: Right! The bonding MO is lowest in energy, and it can hold 2 electrons with opposite spins. It's filled; the antibonding MO stays empty.
explain.mo-split: Electrons fill from the bottom up, and the bonding MO holds two. Putting one in the antibonding MO would cancel out the bond.
explain.mo-both-anti: The antibonding MO is HIGHER in energy, so electrons don't go there first. Both go into the bonding MO.
explain.mo-atomic: That's closer to the valence bond picture. In MO theory, the orbitals belong to the whole molecule, and both electrons sit in the bonding MO.

problems.prompt: How many electrons does selenium (Z = 34) have in its outermost shell? (Problem 1-2c)
problems.hint: Selenium is in group 6A, right under oxygen and sulfur.

explain.ve-6: Right! Selenium's outermost shell is shell 4: 4s² 4p⁴ = 6 electrons. Same as O and S, its group-mates.
explain.ve-16: Tempting if you count 4s² 3d¹⁰ 4p⁴. But 3d belongs to shell 3, not the outermost shell. Only 4s² 4p⁴ count: 6.
explain.ve-34: 34 is selenium's TOTAL electron count (its atomic number). Only the outermost shell, 4s² 4p⁴, counts here: 6.
explain.ve-2: 2 would be just the 4s electrons. Don't forget the 4p⁴: 2 + 4 = 6.

problems.prompt: The two lobes of a p orbital are separated by a 'node.' What is a node?
problems.hint: Electrons are never found there.

explain.node-zero: Right! A node is a region of zero electron density. The lobes on either side of it have opposite algebraic signs (+ and −).
explain.node-nucleus: The p orbital's node does pass through the nucleus, but the node itself is a region of ZERO electron density, not the nucleus.
explain.node-max: Opposite! A node is where electron density is ZERO.
explain.node-overlap: Overlap zones are where bonds form, and electron density there is high. A node has zero density.

lesson.text: Path of Shapes! A puzzle: carbon is 2s² 2p², with two kinds of orbitals. Yet all four C–H bonds in methane are identical. Linus Pauling's answer: the 2s and three 2p orbitals mix into four equal sp³ HYBRID orbitals.

The sp³ hybrids point to the corners of a tetrahedron, 109.5° apart. The '3' means three p orbitals were mixed in. It does NOT count electrons. Hybrids are lopsided, with one big lobe, so they overlap well and form strong bonds.

Mix the 2s with only TWO p's and you get three sp² hybrids in a flat plane, 120° apart, plus one leftover p orbital. In ethylene, the leftover p's overlap SIDEWAYS to make a π bond. Double bond = 1 σ + 1 π.
Mix 2s with just ONE p and you get two sp hybrids, 180° apart, plus two leftover p's. In acetylene those make TWO π bonds. Triple bond = 1 σ + 2 π, and the molecule is linear.

The book's data (Table 1.2): C–C is 153 pm and 377 kJ/mol. C=C is 134 pm and 728 kJ/mol. C≡C is 120 pm and 965 kJ/mol. More bonds means shorter and stronger. But a double bond is less than twice as strong, because sideways π overlap is weaker than head-on σ overlap.
Shortcut: count the groups around the carbon. 4 single bonds → sp³. A double bond → sp². A triple bond (or two double bonds) → sp.

problems.prompt: Match each molecule to the hybridization of its carbons.
problems.hint: Single bonds only → sp³. Double → sp². Triple → sp.

explain.hyb-sp3: sp³ goes with ethane: each carbon has four single (σ) bonds pointing to the corners of a tetrahedron.
explain.hyb-sp2: sp² goes with ethylene: each carbon has three σ bonds in a plane plus a leftover p orbital for the π bond.
explain.hyb-sp: sp goes with acetylene: each carbon has two σ bonds at 180° plus two leftover p orbitals for two π bonds.
explain.hyb-p: Carbon's bonds aren't made from plain p orbitals, which would put them 90° apart. Real carbon bonds use hybrids (sp³, sp², sp).

problems.prompt: What is the H–C–H bond angle in methane, CH₄?
problems.hint: Four sp³ orbitals point to the corners of a tetrahedron.

explain.ang-109: Right! Methane's four sp³ orbitals point to the corners of a regular tetrahedron: 109.5°, the tetrahedral angle.
explain.ang-90: 90° is the angle between plain, unhybridized p orbitals. Carbon uses sp³ hybrids in methane, so the angle is 109.5°.
explain.ang-120: 120° is for sp² carbons (flat, like ethylene). Methane's carbon is sp³: 109.5°.
explain.ang-180: 180° is for linear sp carbons (like acetylene). Methane is tetrahedral: 109.5°.

problems.prompt: What is the geometry around each carbon in ethylene, H₂C=CH₂?
problems.hint: How many sp² hybrids, and how are they arranged?

explain.geo-planar120: Right! Each sp² carbon has three hybrid orbitals in a plane, ~120° apart. The whole ethylene molecule is flat. (Actual angles: 117.4° H–C–H, 121.3° H–C–C.)
explain.geo-tetra: Tetrahedral (109.5°) is for sp³ carbons with four single bonds. Ethylene's carbons are sp², so they're flat with ~120° angles.
explain.geo-linear: Linear (180°) is for sp carbons, like in acetylene's triple bond. Ethylene's double-bond carbons are sp²: flat, ~120°.
explain.geo-square: Carbon never arranges bonds in a 90° square. Ethylene's sp² carbons are trigonal planar, ~120°.

problems.prompt: Rank these carbon–carbon bonds from SHORTEST to LONGEST.
problems.hint: More electrons between the nuclei pull them closer together.
problems.why: More shared electrons pull the nuclei closer: C≡C 120 pm < C=C 134 pm < C–C 153 pm (Table 1.2).

explain.bl-triple: C≡C is 120 pm: the SHORTEST carbon–carbon bond. Six shared electrons hold the nuclei tight.
explain.bl-double: C=C is 134 pm: in the MIDDLE. Four shared electrons.
explain.bl-single: C–C is 153 pm: the LONGEST. Only two shared electrons.

problems.prompt: Rank these carbon–carbon bonds from STRONGEST to WEAKEST.
problems.hint: Shorter bonds are stronger bonds.
problems.why: C≡C 965 kJ/mol > C=C 728 kJ/mol > C–C 377 kJ/mol (Table 1.2).

explain.bl-triple: C≡C is 965 kJ/mol: the STRONGEST carbon–carbon bond (1 σ + 2 π).
explain.bl-double: C=C is 728 kJ/mol: in the MIDDLE (1 σ + 1 π).
explain.bl-single: C–C is 377 kJ/mol: the WEAKEST (just 1 σ).

problems.prompt: A carbon–carbon triple bond is made of...
problems.hint: Only one bond can point straight between the two nuclei.

explain.tb-1s2p: Right! sp–sp head-on overlap gives 1 σ bond. The two leftover p orbitals on each carbon (py and pz) overlap sideways for 2 π bonds.
explain.tb-3s: Only ONE bond can overlap head-on along the line between two nuclei. The other two are sideways π bonds: 1 σ + 2 π.
explain.tb-2s1p: Two atoms can only share one σ bond. A triple bond is 1 σ + 2 π.
explain.tb-3p: Every multiple bond starts with a σ bond. A triple bond is 1 σ + 2 π.

problems.prompt: A C=C bond (728 kJ/mol) is LESS than twice as strong as a C–C bond (377 kJ/mol). Why?
problems.hint: Compare sideways overlap with head-on overlap.

explain.db-pi-weaker: Right! The π part of the double bond comes from sideways p–p overlap, which isn't as effective as σ head-on overlap. So the π bond adds less than a full σ bond's worth.
explain.db-longer: Double bonds are actually SHORTER (134 pm vs 153 pm). The real reason is that the π part's sideways overlap is weaker than σ head-on overlap.
explain.db-two-sigma: A double bond is 1 σ + 1 π, not two σ bonds. The weaker π bond is why it isn't twice as strong.
explain.db-sigma-weak: The σ part is still strong head-on overlap. It's the π part (sideways overlap) that's weaker.

problems.prompt: What does the superscript '3' in sp³ tell you?
problems.hint: It's a recipe: how many of each orbital went in.

explain.sp3-meaning: Right! sp³ means one s orbital and three p orbitals combined. The superscript counts orbitals mixed in, not electrons.
explain.sp3-3e: The book warns about exactly this: the superscript is NOT an electron count. No orbital holds more than 2 electrons. It means three p orbitals mixed in.
explain.sp3-3bonds: An sp³ carbon makes FOUR bonds, one per hybrid. The '3' means three p orbitals were mixed with one s.
explain.sp3-shell3: Carbon's hybrids come from the second shell (2s, 2p). The '3' counts the p orbitals mixed in.

lesson.text: Hybridization isn't just for carbon! Look at the nitrogen in methylamine, CH₃NH₂. Its bond angles are 107–110°, close to tetrahedral. So nitrogen is sp³ too: three hybrids form bonds, and the fourth holds a LONE PAIR.
The big lesson: lone pairs count as groups! They take up a hybrid orbital just like a bond does. Oxygen in methanol: 2 bonds + 2 lone pairs = 4 groups → sp³. The C–O–H angle is 108.5°.
Phosphorus and sulfur are third-row cousins of N and O. They can expand their octets: P often makes 5 bonds, S often makes 4. In methyl phosphate, the O–P–O angles are 110–112°, so P is sp³.
Bigger molecules? Go atom by atom. In propene, CH₃–CH=CH₂, the CH₃ carbon is sp³ and both double-bond carbons are sp². In propyne, CH₃–C≡CH, the CH₃ is sp³ and both triple-bond carbons are sp.

Count groups (bonds + lone pairs, with a double or triple bond counting as ONE group): 4 groups → sp³ (109.5°), 3 groups → sp² (120°), 2 groups → sp (180°). It even works on odd species like a carbocation, CH₃⁺: 3 groups → sp², flat.

problems.prompt: What is the hybridization of the nitrogen in methylamine, CH₃NH₂?
problems.hint: Don't forget nitrogen's lone pair. Count it as a group.

explain.hyb-sp3: Right! N has 3 bonds + 1 lone pair = 4 groups → sp³. Its bond angles (107.1°, 110.3°) are close to tetrahedral.
explain.hyb-sp2: That's what you get if you count only the 3 bonds. The lone pair takes a hybrid orbital too: 4 groups → sp³.
explain.hyb-sp: sp is for 2 groups (like a triple-bond carbon). Nitrogen here has 3 bonds + 1 lone pair = 4 groups → sp³.
explain.hyb-none: Nitrogen does hybridize! Its tetrahedral-ish bond angles tell us it's sp³.

problems.prompt: Describe the oxygen atom in methanol, CH₃OH.
problems.hint: O has 6 valence electrons and makes 2 bonds.

explain.lp-sp3-2: Right! O makes 2 bonds (to C and H) and keeps 4 electrons as 2 lone pairs. 4 groups → sp³, with a C–O–H angle of 108.5°.
explain.lp-sp3-1: Oxygen has 6 valence electrons. 2 go into bonds and 4 are left = 2 lone pairs. (1 lone pair is nitrogen's pattern.)
explain.lp-sp2-2: sp² would mean 3 groups. Oxygen here has 2 bonds + 2 lone pairs = 4 groups → sp³.
explain.lp-sp-2: sp gives only 2 hybrid orbitals, which isn't enough room for 2 bonds and 2 lone pairs. It's 4 groups → sp³.

problems.prompt: Propene, CH₃–CH=CH₂ (Problem 1-10). Give each carbon's hybridization.
problems.hint: Both carbons of a double bond have the same hybridization.

explain.hyb-sp3: sp³ fits the CH₃ carbon: four single bonds, ~109° angles. The double-bond carbons are sp².
explain.hyb-sp2: sp² fits BOTH double-bond carbons: three σ bonds in a plane (~120°) plus a p orbital for the π bond.
explain.hyb-sp: There's no triple bond (or two double bonds on one carbon) in propene, so no sp carbons. CH₃ is sp³, and the C=C carbons are sp².

problems.prompt: Propyne, CH₃–C≡CH (Problem 1-13). Give each carbon's hybridization.
problems.hint: Triple-bond carbons have two groups each.

explain.hyb-sp3: sp³ fits the CH₃ carbon: four single bonds. The triple-bond carbons are sp.
explain.hyb-sp: sp fits BOTH triple-bond carbons: two σ bonds at 180° (C≡C–C and H–C≡C are linear) plus two p orbitals for the two π bonds.
explain.hyb-sp2: sp² is for double-bond carbons. Propyne has a triple bond, so those carbons are sp. The CH₃ is sp³.

problems.prompt: In methyl phosphate, CH₃OPO₃²⁻, the O–P–O bond angles are about 110–112°. What hybridization does that suggest for phosphorus?
problems.hint: Which hybridization has angles near 109.5°?

explain.hyb-sp3: Right! Angles of 110–112° are close to the 109.5° tetrahedral angle, which implies sp³ phosphorus with four groups (the four oxygens).
explain.hyb-sp2: sp² would give 120° angles in a flat arrangement. The measured 110–112° points to sp³.
explain.hyb-sp: sp would give a 180° linear shape. 110–112° is nearly tetrahedral → sp³.
explain.hyb-none: Phosphorus hybridizes just like nitrogen does. The near-tetrahedral angles say sp³.

problems.prompt: What shape is the C–O–C part of dimethyl ether, CH₃–O–CH₃? (Problem 1-14a)
problems.hint: Oxygen has 2 bonds and 2 lone pairs.

explain.geo-bent: Right! O has 2 bonds + 2 lone pairs = 4 groups → sp³. The lone pairs fill two corners of the tetrahedron, so the C–O–C bonds are bent at a near-tetrahedral angle.
explain.geo-linear: Linear would ignore oxygen's 2 lone pairs. They count as groups: 4 groups → sp³, so the C–O–C is bent.
explain.geo-planar120: Flat 120° means 3 groups (sp²). Oxygen here has 4 groups (2 bonds + 2 lone pairs) → sp³, bent.
explain.geo-square: No 90° squares here. 4 groups around O → sp³ tetrahedral arrangement → bent C–O–C.

problems.prompt: What is the shape of benzene, and how are its carbons hybridized? (Problem 1-36)
problems.hint: Every carbon is part of a C=C double bond.

explain.benz-planar-sp2: Right! Every carbon is in a double bond with 3 groups → sp². Their 120° angles fit perfectly into a flat hexagon.
explain.benz-pucker-sp3: sp³ carbons have only single bonds. Every benzene carbon is in a C=C double bond, so they're all sp² and the ring is flat.
explain.benz-planar-sp: sp carbons are linear (180°), and you can't bend those into a ring. Benzene's carbons are sp² (120°).
explain.benz-alt: The drawing alternates single and double bonds, but EVERY carbon is part of one double bond, so every carbon is sp².

problems.prompt: A carbocation like CH₃⁺ has a positive carbon with only 3 bonds and no lone pairs. What hybridization and shape do you expect? (Problem 1-49)
problems.hint: Count the groups on the carbon. An empty orbital isn't a group.

explain.cat-sp2: Right! 3 groups → three sp² hybrids in a flat plane (120°), with one EMPTY p orbital left over. The positive carbon has 6 valence electrons.
explain.cat-sp3: sp³ needs 4 groups. CH₃⁺ has only 3 bonds and no lone pair, so it's sp² and flat. The empty orbital is a leftover p.
explain.cat-sp: sp is for 2 groups. CH₃⁺ has 3 bonds → sp², trigonal planar.

lesson.text: Path of Drawing! Drawing every C and H gets tiring, so chemists use shortcuts. A CONDENSED structure skips the bond lines: CH₃CH₂CH₃. A SKELETAL structure goes further and hides the C's and H's completely.

Skeletal Rule 1: a carbon sits at every line END and every place lines MEET. Rule 2: H's on carbon aren't drawn. Each carbon has 4 bonds, so you fill in the missing H's yourself. Rule 3: any atom other than C or H IS drawn, along with H's attached to it (like –OH).
Counting H's: a line END has 1 bond drawn → CH₃. A two-way corner → CH₂. A three-way junction → CH. A four-way junction → C with no H. Every double bond line counts as 2 bonds!
Worked example: 2-methylbutane, above. It has 5 carbons. Two ends on the left (2 × CH₃), one three-way junction (CH), one corner (CH₂), and one more end (CH₃). H's: 3+3+1+2+3 = 12. Formula: C₅H₁₂.
Handy check: an open chain with only single bonds has 2n+2 H's (n = number of carbons). Each ring or double bond takes away 2 H's. Methylcyclohexane: 7 carbons, 1 ring → 16 − 2 = 14 → C₇H₁₄.

problems.prompt: In a skeletal structure, where are the carbon atoms?
problems.hint: Rule 1 has two parts.

explain.skel-ends: Right! Rule 1: a carbon is at every intersection of lines AND at the end of every line.
explain.skel-written: In skeletal structures, carbons usually AREN'T written. They're understood to be at every line end and intersection.
explain.skel-endsonly: That misses the carbons where lines meet. Carbons are at line ends AND intersections.
explain.skel-cornersonly: That misses the carbons at line ends (usually CH₃ groups). Carbons are at ends AND intersections.

problems.prompt: What is the molecular formula of this compound (2-methylbutane)?
problems.hint: Count carbons (line ends + junctions), then H's using 4 bonds per carbon.

explain.mf-c5h12: Right! 5 carbons: 3 line ends (CH₃ ×3 = 9 H), 1 three-way junction (CH = 1 H), 1 corner (CH₂ = 2 H). 9 + 1 + 2 = 12. Check: 2(5)+2 = 12 ✓.
explain.mf-c5h10: C₅H₁₀ would need a ring or a double bond. This structure is an open chain with only single bonds: C₅H₁₂ (2n+2).
explain.mf-c4h10: Don't forget the branch! The methyl sticking off the chain is a carbon too. 4 in the main chain + 1 branch = 5 carbons: C₅H₁₂.
explain.mf-c5h11: An odd H count on a neutral hydrocarbon leaves some carbon without 4 bonds. Recount: 3 CH₃ + 1 CH + 1 CH₂ = 12 H.

problems.prompt: What is the molecular formula of isoprene? (Table 1.3)
problems.hint: Each double bond line counts as 2 bonds for that carbon.

explain.mf-c5h8: Right! 5 carbons and two C=C double bonds. Each double bond removes 2 H's from the 2n+2 max: 12 − 4 = 8. C₅H₈.
explain.mf-c5h12: That's the count for an all-single-bond chain. Isoprene has TWO double bonds, each costing 2 H's: 12 − 4 = 8.
explain.mf-c5h10: That accounts for only one double bond. Isoprene has two: 12 − 2 − 2 = 8 → C₅H₈.
explain.mf-c4h6: Don't skip the methyl branch. That's a fifth carbon. 5 carbons, two double bonds → C₅H₈.

problems.prompt: What is the molecular formula of methylcyclohexane? (Table 1.3)
problems.hint: 6 ring carbons + 1 methyl. A ring costs 2 H's.

explain.mf-c7h14: Right! 7 carbons. Ring: 5 CH₂ + 1 CH. Methyl: 1 CH₃. H's: 10 + 1 + 3 = 14. Check: 2(7)+2 − 2 (ring) = 14 ✓.
explain.mf-c7h16: That's an open chain (heptane). Closing the ring uses up one more bond, which removes 2 H's: C₇H₁₄.
explain.mf-c6h12: That's cyclohexane alone. Don't forget the methyl branch: 7 carbons total → C₇H₁₄.
explain.mf-c7h12: That would need a ring AND a double bond (or two rings). Methylcyclohexane has one ring and no double bonds: C₇H₁₄.

problems.prompt: How many H's does a carbon carry at each spot in a skeletal structure? (Single bonds only.)
problems.hint: 4 bonds total minus the bonds you can see = number of H's.

explain.hc-ch3: CH₃ is a line END: 1 bond drawn, so 4 − 1 = 3 H's.
explain.hc-ch2: CH₂ is a two-way corner: 2 bonds drawn, so 2 H's.
explain.hc-ch: CH is a three-way junction: 3 bonds drawn, so 1 H.
explain.hc-c: A plain C is a four-way junction: all 4 bonds drawn, no room for H.
explain.hc-ch4: CH₄ (methane) has no C–C bonds at all, so it isn't any of these spots. A carbon in a skeleton always has at least 1 line drawn.

problems.prompt: What is the molecular formula of phenol? (Table 1.3)
problems.hint: Skeletal structures DO show H's on oxygen.

explain.mf-c6h6o: Right! 6 ring carbons: 5 of them are CH (each has a double bond + 2 ring bonds), and 1 carries the OH. 5 + 1 (the O–H) = 6 H. C₆H₆O.
explain.mf-c6h5o: Don't forget the H on the oxygen. It's part of the –OH group. 5 ring H's + 1 = 6: C₆H₆O.
explain.mf-c6h12o: That ignores the three double bonds. Each double bond line counts as 2 bonds, so the ring carbons have only one H each: C₆H₆O.
explain.mf-c6h6: Rule 3: atoms other than C and H are shown, so that O counts! C₆H₆O.

problems.prompt: In a skeletal structure, which atoms are actually written out?
problems.hint: Rules 2 and 3.

explain.skel-hetero: Right! Rule 3: atoms other than C and H are written. H's bonded to those atoms are written too (–OH, –NH₂). Only C's and their H's are hidden.
explain.skel-onlyc: Backwards! Carbons are the atoms that AREN'T written in skeletal structures (Rule 1).
explain.skel-every: Writing every atom is a line-bond (Kekulé) structure. Skeletal structures hide C's and the H's on C.
explain.skel-charged: Every heteroatom (O, N, Cl, etc.) is written whether or not it's charged.

lesson.text: Now let's go the other way: from a formula to a drawing. The rules don't change. C makes 4 bonds, N makes 3, O makes 2, and H and halogens make 1. Snap atoms together until every atom is happy.

Some formulas have more than one answer! C₄H₁₀ can be a straight chain (butane) or branched (isobutane). C₂H₆O can be ethanol (CH₃CH₂OH) or dimethyl ether (CH₃OCH₃). Same atoms, different connections, different compounds.
Use the H count as a clue. For n carbons, a chain with only single bonds has 2n+2 H's. Two fewer H's means ONE ring or ONE double bond. C₃H₆ can be propene (double bond) or cyclopropane (ring).
Reading condensed structures: (CH₃)₂CH– means a CH with two CH₃ groups hanging off it. So (CH₃)₂CHCH₂CH₃ is a 4-carbon chain with a branch on carbon 2: 2-methylbutane, C₅H₁₂.
And if a formula breaks the rules, like CH₅ (carbon would need 5 bonds), it can't exist. Valence rules are your best friend.

problems.prompt: Which skeletal structure is butane, CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₃?
problems.hint: Four carbons in a row, all single bonds.

explain.s-butane: Right! A zigzag with 4 carbons (2 ends + 2 corners), all single bonds. C₄H₁₀.
explain.s-isobutane: Same formula (C₄H₁₀), but branched: three carbons hang off one central CH. Butane is an unbranched chain of 4.
explain.s-propane: Count the carbons: only 3 (2 ends + 1 corner). Butane has 4.
explain.s-1butene: 4 carbons, but there's a double bond (C₄H₈). Butane has only single bonds.

problems.prompt: C₂H₆O has two possible structures (Problem 1-54). Pick the one where oxygen is bonded to TWO carbons.
problems.hint: The O should sit in the middle of the chain, not at the end.

explain.s-dme: Right! Dimethyl ether, CH₃–O–CH₃: oxygen in the middle with 2 bonds to carbons. C₂H₆O.
explain.s-ethanol: Ethanol IS C₂H₆O, the other isomer! But its O is bonded to one C and one H (an –OH). The C–O–C one is dimethyl ether.
explain.s-acetaldehyde: The C=O double bond costs 2 H's: this is C₂H₄O, not C₂H₆O.
explain.s-methanol: Only one carbon here: CH₄O. We need two carbons.

problems.prompt: Match each description to its structure. (Based on Problem 1-53.)
problems.hint: Max H for 3 carbons is 8. Each ring or double bond removes 2.

explain.s-propene: Propene, CH₂=CHCH₃: 3 carbons, one double bond → 8 − 2 = 6 H. It's the 'C₃H₆ with a double bond.'
explain.s-cyclopropane: Cyclopropane: 3 CH₂ in a ring → 6 H. It's the 'C₃H₆ with a ring.'
explain.s-propane: Propane, CH₃CH₂CH₃: all single bonds, no ring → 2(3)+2 = 8 H. It's C₃H₈.
explain.s-propyne: Propyne has a triple bond, which costs 4 H's: C₃H₄. It doesn't match any of these.

problems.prompt: Which structure has the formula CH₅N? (Problem 1-30b)
problems.hint: C makes 4 bonds and N makes 3. Fill the rest with H's.

explain.s-methylamine: Right! Methylamine, CH₃–NH₂: C has 3 H's + 1 bond to N, and N has 2 H's + 1 bond to C. 3 + 2 = 5 H.
explain.s-methanimine: The C=N double bond uses up extra bonds: CH₂=NH is CH₃N, two H's short.
explain.s-methanediamine: Two nitrogens: CH₆N₂. We need just one N.
explain.s-methanol: That's an O, not an N: CH₃OH is CH₄O.

problems.prompt: Which skeletal structure matches the condensed structure (CH₃)₂CHCH₂CH₃?
problems.hint: (CH₃)₂CH– is a CH carrying two CH₃ groups.

explain.s-2mebutane: Right! (CH₃)₂CH is a carbon with two methyls, then CH₂, then CH₃. That's a 4-carbon chain with a methyl on C2: 2-methylbutane.
explain.s-pentane: Pentane is unbranched: CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂CH₃. The (CH₃)₂CH part means a branch point.
explain.s-neopentane: This has a central C with FOUR CH₃ groups, C(CH₃)₄. Ours has a CH with only two methyls, then a CH₂CH₃.
explain.s-isobutane: Isobutane, (CH₃)₂CHCH₃, has only 4 carbons. Ours has an extra CH₂: 5 carbons.

problems.prompt: Which structure is vinyl chloride, C₂H₃Cl, the starting material for PVC? (Problem 1-27)
problems.hint: Two carbons with only 3 H's + 1 Cl means there's a double bond.

explain.s-vinylcl: Right! CH₂=CHCl. Two carbons with a double bond leave 4 spots: 3 H + 1 Cl.
explain.s-chloroethane: No double bond, so there's room for 5 H's + Cl: C₂H₅Cl.
explain.s-dichloroethene: Two chlorines: C₂H₂Cl₂. We need one Cl and three H's.
explain.s-chloroacetylene: A triple bond leaves only 2 spots: C₂HCl. We need a double bond for C₂H₃Cl.

problems.prompt: Why can't a molecule with the formula CH₅ exist? (Problem 1-25a)
problems.hint: Each H makes one bond to carbon.

explain.ch5-5bonds: Right! Each H forms one bond, so 5 H's would need 5 bonds to carbon. Carbon forms only 4, so CH₄ is the max.
explain.ch5-hneeds2: Hydrogen forms just one bond. The problem is carbon: 5 H's would need 5 bonds, and carbon only makes 4.
explain.ch5-toolight: Small molecules are fine (CH₄ is smaller!). The problem is that carbon would need 5 bonds.
explain.ch5-noh: C–H bonds are strong (about 439 kJ/mol in methane). The problem is that carbon would need 5 bonds.

intro.speaker: boss
intro.text: So. Another little student climbing MY tower. Dott still drawing his precious dots, is he?

intro.speaker: npc
intro.text: Mordant! This student actually understands WHY carbon forms four bonds. You can't scare that out of them.

intro.speaker: boss
intro.text: Understanding is slow. Memorize, child! 'Carbon: four. Double bond: sp².' Why bother asking why? Let's see how you do when I scramble everything you've learned!

wrong: Ha! See? You should have just memorized it.
Why, why, why... and still wrong!
My flashcards never lie. You, however...
right: Hmph. Dott's dots won't save you forever.
Fine. But can you do it again?

defeat.speaker: boss
defeat.text: Impossible... you reasoned it out? Every single one?

defeat.speaker: npc
defeat.text: That's the difference, Mordant. Memorized answers crumble when the question changes. Understanding doesn't.

defeat.speaker: boss
defeat.text: Enjoy your little victory. The next floor's teacher has a temper, and I have a few acid tricks waiting for you...

story.speaker: narrator
story.text: Mordant's ghost dissolves into green smoke. For a moment, the cracked flask he always carries glows. It's labeled 'H⁺'.

story.speaker: npc
story.text: Take this lantern, my student. It holds the light of understanding. When you're truly stuck, it can show you an answer AND explain why it's right.

story.speaker: narrator
story.text: A spiral staircase unfolds above you. From somewhere upstairs, a voice bellows: 'DROP AND GIVE ME A PROTON!' Floor 2 awaits.

legendary.name: Dott's Lantern
legendary.desc: Fills one empty slot with the correct card and explains why it's right. Won from Floor 1's boss.

problems.prompt: Acetonitrile, CH₃–C≡N (Problems 1-26 and 1-34). Fill in each blank.
problems.hint: N in a triple bond uses 3 of its 5 electrons for bonding.

explain.hyb-sp3: sp³ is the CH₃ carbon: four single bonds.
explain.hyb-sp: sp is the nitrile carbon: it's in a triple bond, with 2 groups (the CH₃ and the N) at 180°.
explain.hyb-sp2: No double bonds here. CH₃ is sp³ and the C≡N carbon is sp.
explain.lp-1: N has 5 valence electrons. 3 go into the triple bond (6 shared electrons), leaving 2 = one lone pair. N's outer shell: 6 bonding + 2 nonbonding = 8.
explain.lp-2: Two lone pairs is oxygen's pattern. Nitrogen in C≡N uses 3 electrons for bonding and keeps 2: one lone pair.

problems.prompt: Allene, H₂C=C=CH₂, has two double bonds on its central carbon (Problem 1-46). What is the central carbon's hybridization?
problems.hint: Count the groups on the central carbon. Each double bond counts as one.

explain.hyb-sp: Right! The central carbon has 2 groups (two double bonds) → sp, linear (180°). Its two leftover p orbitals each make one of the π bonds. (The end carbons are sp².)
explain.hyb-sp2: Tempting, since it's in double bonds! But it's in TWO of them, so it has only 2 groups → sp. Only the end CH₂ carbons are sp².
explain.hyb-sp3: sp³ is for four single bonds. The central carbon has two double bonds → 2 groups → sp.

problems.prompt: What is the hybridization of carbon in carbon dioxide, O=C=O? (Problem 1-47)
problems.hint: Same idea as allene's middle carbon.

explain.hyb-sp: Right! Carbon has two double bonds = 2 groups → sp, and CO₂ is linear (180°). Two leftover p orbitals form the two C=O π bonds.
explain.hyb-sp2: Two double bonds means only 2 groups on carbon → sp, linear. sp² would mean 3 groups.
explain.hyb-sp3: sp³ needs 4 groups. Carbon in CO₂ has 2 (two double bonds) → sp.
explain.hyb-p: Carbon uses hybrids here: sp for the σ bonds, plus two unhybridized p orbitals for the π bonds.

problems.prompt: Put these orbitals in the order they FILL, first to last.
problems.hint: The book says the 4s orbital lies between 3p and 3d in energy.
problems.why: Aufbau order: ...3s, 3p, 4s, 3d, 4p. The 4s is lower in energy than 3d, so it fills first.

explain.orb-3p: 3p fills right after 3s and comes FIRST of these.
explain.orb-4s: 4s is sneaky. It's lower in energy than 3d, so it fills SECOND, between 3p and 3d.
explain.orb-3d: 3d fills THIRD, after 4s, even though it's in shell 3.
explain.orb-4p: 4p fills after 3d, so it comes after all three of these. It doesn't belong in this sequence.

problems.prompt: Carvone gives spearmint its smell (Worked Example 1.4). What is its molecular formula?
problems.hint: 10 carbons. Count: 1 ring + 3 double bonds (two C=C, one C=O).

explain.mf-c10h14o: Right! 10 carbons. Max H for 10 C is 22. The ring and the three double bonds (two C=C, one C=O) each remove 2: 22 − 8 = 14. Plus 1 O. C₁₀H₁₄O.
explain.mf-c10h16o: One double bond short. Carvone has a ring + two C=C + one C=O = 4 'H-removers' → 22 − 8 = 14 H.
explain.mf-c10h14: Rule 3: heteroatoms are drawn, so that O counts. C₁₀H₁₄O.
explain.mf-c9h14o: Recount carbons. Don't miss the CH₂ at the end of the isopropenyl group's double bond. 10 carbons: C₁₀H₁₄O.
